# Afterword {.unnumbered}

The 1446 book closed with a postface, and it made two claims for its little
alphabet. The first was that a wise man could learn it before the morning was
over, and a slow one within ten days. The second was that it could write down
any sound at all: the wind, the cry of a crane, the crowing of a cock, the
barking of a dog. This book closes by restating both, because they are its own
measures of success.

## The ten-day challenge

The first claim was about speed, and you have finished its morning. Here is the
rest of the promise. For the next ten days, bring one question a day from *your
own data*, not from the book's cast of tables, and answer it in one sentence.
Start where the [cookbook](parts/cookbook.qmd) starts: what shape is your data,
and what do you want to know? By day three the recipes will read as ordinary
sentences, because you will already know every word in them. By day ten you
should be writing sentences this book never showed you. That is the one outcome
that proves you learned the grammar and not the examples.

Two things count as a surprise. A sentence renders when you expected a refusal,
or it refuses and gives you a direction you disagree with. Either is worth
reporting, because a grammar this small stays correct only when its readers say
where it is wrong.

## Growth without new words

The second claim was about reach: any sound at all. A grammar of graphics
answers it in pictures, and the kernel you learned is the whole vocabulary it
has. The engine draws every word in it: every mark, every channel, every
transform, every space, and the one selection. Not every *pairing* of words is
drawn yet, and [Combinations](combinations.qmd) is the page that lists the ones
the engine still refuses. No word is waiting.

Growth arrives as new pictures rather than new words. The **choropleth** is the
pattern, and no atom was added for it. It shades each country by a value. What
it needed was not a new word but a new shape of table: one row for every point
along a country's border. A `zone` is a filled region, and five different things
can fix where its edges are. A **boundary** is the fifth, and `group` already
says which rows belong to one country. [Map](map.qmd) shows the choropleth drawn
with the words the kernel already had.

The vocabulary does not grow across languages either. Whatever sentence you
write becomes one small specification inside the package, and all four bindings
build the same one from the same words. What differs is how each one names a
column, and JavaScript spells the operators as words as well, because it cannot
overload them. Each binding has a short chapter of its own, a difference list:
[R](bindings/r.qmd), [Python](bindings/python.qmd), [Julia](bindings/julia.qmd),
[JavaScript](bindings/javascript.qmd).

```python
# Python
(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life)
  + color(col.continent))
```

```julia
# Julia
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + color(:continent)
```

```js
// JavaScript
plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life), color(col.continent))
```

## One goal left

Those four spellings are finished work. One thing this project set out to do is
not, and it is written down here so you can check later whether the project did
it. Half of it already works: the engine itself runs inside the page, which is
how a 3-D plot turns when you drag it in the web edition. The other half is
every example in this book, editable in place. Change `color(continent)` to
`shape(continent)`, and watch the plot redraw. The book you are reading is ready
for that change today, because it holds no saved pictures: every plot in it
comes from a specification the engine reads.

## Writing quickly is not writing well

I think Hangeul (한글) is a perfect writing system. I should admit that I may be
biased, because it is the alphabet I write with. What nobody disputes is that
it is fast to read and fast to write.

Writing quickly is not the same as writing well. There is no quick route to
good writing: you read good writing, and you practice. Visualization is no
different. This tool is new and it has problems, and what I hope it can be for
now is a good tool to practice with.

The same division sits in the 1446 story. King Sejong made the alphabet. He did
not write the books that were written with it. I am not a great author of plots
either. What I do have is twenty years in this field as a user, watching and
listening and reading. I built from that experience, and what came out is a tool
that is easy to learn and easy to use.

I hope good work comes out of it.

## The gap

A specification is a sentence said before the picture exists. Everyone who
writes one waits in that gap, between declaring what they want to see and
finding out whether the engine agrees. The package is `gog`. The state of
working with it is *agog*. I hope the book kept you there.
